title: Kidney replacement that is portable and affordable at global scale

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a complete kidney-replacement service that people can use at home or in resource-constrained settings, with adequate removal of excess fluid and waste solutes and substantially lower demands for water, power, consumables, specialist staff and infrastructure. Portability is one requirement; the larger goal is dependable, affordable treatment that local services can sustain at population scale. This defines the target capability, rather than an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Wearable dialysis with regenerated dialysate provides one technical route. A sorbent-based system recirculates a small dialysate volume through materials that remove waste, while battery-powered pumping supports treatment away from stationary equipment. The supplied human study demonstrates elements of this approach. Completing the concept also requires safe treatment access, infection prevention, reliable alarms, usable controls, maintenance, repairs and dependable supplies. The service need not be implanted or reproduce every biological kidney function.

significance.text: If safe and inexpensive treatment could operate without a specialized dialysis center or large supplies of purified water, it could reduce location and infrastructure barriers to life-sustaining kidney replacement. The revolutionary consequence would be expanded access and greater freedom over where treatment occurs. Demonstrated wearable fluid and solute removal provides a technical basis for this possibility, but the supplied trial does not establish expanded access, affordability or improved population outcomes.

As a conditional service-level synthesis, successful deployment could make treatment feasible in more communities and reduce dependence on repeated travel to centralized facilities. These benefits would still depend on financing, safe access care, patient and caregiver support, maintenance and reliable supply chains. Moving equipment into the home can redistribute work and costs rather than eliminate them, so portability alone is insufficient evidence of affordability or global scalability.

The analogy to a biological kidney has important limits. This concept targets practical replacement of enough fluid and solute regulation to sustain patients; it does not require restoration of all kidney functions or independence from other medical care. Its impact should therefore be judged by clinical outcomes, treatment burden and access, rather than by resemblance to an intact organ.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central engineering challenge is sustained, reliable fluid and solute control in a compact system suitable for independent use. In the supplied wearable trial, excessive carbon dioxide bubbles in the dialysate circuit and variable blood and dialysate flows contributed to stopping the study. These findings identify concrete barriers in gas management, pumping and circuit reliability. Sorbent regeneration and miniaturization must work together without compromising controlled treatment delivery.

Safe operation outside intensive supervision remains a distinct challenge. The study identified a need for longer outpatient and home studies, including assessment during walking and operation by patients. Reliable alarms, understandable controls, safe access and infection prevention must support treatment under everyday conditions. Short supervised operation cannot establish the long-term safety of continuous treatment or the ability of patients and caregivers to manage it independently.

For the proposed global service, the additional unresolved capability is maintaining clinical performance while reducing total resource requirements and cost. Consumables, staffing, repairs, training and supply continuity must remain manageable in the intended settings. These are proposed engineering and service requirements, not findings of the 2016 trial. The supplied evidence does not establish whether the complete capability remains unavailable as of November 2026.

current_state.text: Gura and colleagues’ study, published in JCI Insight on June 2, 2016, evaluated a wearable sorbent-based artificial kidney in seven participants. Five completed the planned 24 hours of treatment. The trial stopped after the seventh participant because of device-related technical problems, including excessive carbon dioxide bubbles in the dialysate circuit and variable blood and dialysate flows. The result demonstrates short-term wearable treatment functions while exposing reliability problems; it does not demonstrate a completed replacement service.

The system used sorbent regeneration and battery-powered pumping, with an approximate blood-circuit volume of 65 mL and dialysate-circuit volume of 375 mL. Observed fluid and solute removal and the small regenerated dialysate circuit support the technical feasibility of compact treatment. Circuit volume, however, is not a measurement of total treatment water consumption and cannot establish water savings or affordability across the whole service.

The trial involved intensive inpatient monitoring, and participants received conventional dialysis before exposure to the wearable device. Its short duration and treatment context limit conclusions about sustained standalone performance. The authors explicitly identified long-term safety as unestablished and called for longer outpatient and home studies. The study did not establish long-term independent home use, total treatment costs or population-scale delivery.

The supplied research mentions a reported 2026 dialysate-free rabbit prototype, but provides no inspectable source or search entry supporting that report. Its findings and publication status therefore remain unverified here. The claimed earlier publisher-access failure is also not documented in the supplied evidence. These limitations do not show that the prototype report is false, and they do not weaken the documented 2016 results. The empty freshness search record leaves the broader field’s status as of November 2026 unassessed.

According to the supplied review, the evidence assessment covered the full main article in retained HTML and a 15-page PDF, rather than only its abstract. Linked supplements and figure images were not inspected. The quantitative details retained here were supported by article prose, so they do not require interpretation of those uninspected materials.

completion_criteria.text: A proposed convincing clinical demonstration would establish sustained safety and effectiveness during outpatient and independent home use, with outcomes competitive with an appropriate available dialysis comparator. It should measure fluid and solute control, clinically consequential complications, treatment interruptions and the ability of patients and caregivers to operate the system. Longer home evaluation follows directly from limitations identified in the supplied trial; the final study design would need prespecified follow-up duration, endpoints and comparator margins.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained outpatient and home outcomes competitive with appropriate dialysis

completion_criteria.text: For the affordability and scale objective, proposed demonstrations should include diverse settings, including low-resource services, and independent audits of total treatment costs and resource use. Accounting should cover equipment, consumables, water, power, access care, staffing, training, maintenance, repairs and patient or caregiver work. Local teams should demonstrate dependable procurement, fault response and continued treatment delivery. These are proposed criteria for this concept, not established consensus standards or conclusions of the wearable trial.
completion_criteria.label: Audited costs and resource use across dependable low-resource services

completion_criteria.text: Independent replication across sites and operators should establish how performance varies with patient needs and service conditions. Evaluations should report eligibility restrictions, required backup care, failure modes and settings where the service cannot operate safely or economically. Reliability and affordability thresholds must be specified before evaluation. Successful finite studies would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, rather than literal suitability for every patient or health system.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication defines limits against prespecified reliability and affordability thresholds

related_concepts.text: Based on the supplied roster, NEP-04, “A durable, implantable artificial kidney,” is the closest overlap: both pursue artificial replacement of kidney functions. NEP-04 makes durable implantation central, whereas NEP-05 makes portability, affordability and scalable service delivery central and can use an external device. An implantable approach could contribute to NEP-05 if it met its access and cost requirements, but neither concept’s completion would automatically establish the other.

NEP-01, regrowing functional nephrons, and NEP-02, reversing established fibrosis, aim to restore function within existing kidneys. NEP-03, manufacturing transplantable human kidneys, and NEP-06, supplying durable animal-donor kidneys, pursue biological replacement organs. NEP-07 addresses donor-specific immune tolerance in kidney recipients. These concepts overlap with NEP-05 in their ultimate treatment goals, while pursuing different biological capabilities and delivery requirements.

NEP-08, a durable root-cause treatment for ADPKD; NEP-09, durable reversal of diabetic kidney disease; and NEP-10, broad prevention of severe acute kidney injury, target disease treatment or injury prevention. Success could reduce the need for kidney replacement among affected patients. NEP-05 instead addresses provision of replacement therapy when it is needed. These distinctions follow from the supplied roster titles; they do not establish the detailed scope or progress of those entries.

unresolved_issues: The complete capability’s availability and the broader field’s status as of November 2026 remain unassessed by the supplied freshness record.
The identity, findings and publication status of the reported 2026 dialysate-free rabbit prototype, and the claimed prior publisher-access failure, remain unverified.
Long-term clinical performance, independent home reliability, whole-service water and power requirements, affordability and scalable delivery are not established by the supplied trial.
Proposed evaluations still require follow-up duration, clinical endpoints, comparator margins, cost boundaries and reliability thresholds; no numerical resolutions are supplied.

Related-concept distinctions are limited to the supplied roster titles. The review’s recommendation to remove the NEP-04 comparison was not adopted because that title now supports a bounded comparison, without establishing NEP-04’s detailed scope.

brief.title: Portable kidney care people can afford worldwide
possible: People whose kidneys have failed could receive dependable, affordable treatment at home or in communities with limited resources. A portable system would remove excess fluid and waste from their blood while needing much less water, power, equipment and specialist support.
why: This could bring life-sustaining treatment to communities that cannot support a specialist treatment center. Patients could spend less time traveling for care and have more freedom over where treatment happens.

sources.who: Victor Gura, Matthew B. Rivara and colleagues
sources.showed: A wearable device removed excess fluid and waste during a closely supervised hospital trial involving seven people. Gas bubbles and unstable flows caused technical problems that stopped the trial.
sources.cited_for: The trial demonstrated short-term wearable treatment and exposed reliability problems.
sources.not_established: It did not establish sustained independent home treatment, affordability or dependable delivery at scale.

sources.showed: A preliminary conference report described assisted treatment in centers for 29 participants. Blood chemistry stayed generally stable, with no serious adverse device effects (SADEs), meaning serious harm caused by the device.
sources.quote: No SADEs or device deficiencies with potential to cause a serious adverse event occurred.
sources.cited_for: Repeated treatment with a portable system showed encouraging short-term safety under staff supervision.
sources.not_established: The preliminary study had no comparison group and did not establish independent home use, long-term safety or affordability.

sources.showed: A conference report described a trial involving three patients. A portable system removed waste comparably to conventional dialysis, a treatment that filters blood, during brief sessions.
sources.quote:
All patients tolerated and completed treatment with Neokidney
TM
with no adverse events.
sources.cited_for: The small trial supported the feasibility of portable treatment that recycles its cleaning fluid.
sources.not_established: Participants also received conventional treatment, so the trial did not establish sustained treatment with the portable device alone.

shown: Gura and colleagues demonstrated that a wearable device could remove fluid and waste in a closely monitored trial involving seven people. Technical problems stopped the study.

Bolhuis and colleagues reported repeated assisted treatment with the portable Neokidney system in 29 participants. This preliminary conference report extends experience beyond a brief demonstration, but treatment still took place in centers with staff assistance.
missing: Long-term independent home treatment has yet to demonstrate safety and effectiveness comparable to appropriate available dialysis.
Compact systems still need dependable pumps, gas control, alarms and safe connections to patients, with protection against infection.
Affordable services still need to demonstrate lower total resource use, reliable supplies, local repairs and manageable work for patients and caregivers.

milestones.label: Sustained home treatment with competitive health outcomes
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to show sustained safety and effectiveness in outpatient and independent home use, comparable to appropriate dialysis. This would establish that patients and caregivers can manage dependable treatment.

milestones.label: Audited affordability and dependable care in low-resource settings
milestones.explanation: Independent audits across diverse services, including low-resource settings, would have to measure all costs and resources alongside dependable delivery. This would establish whether local teams can sustain affordable care.

milestones.label: Independent replication establishes where treatment works
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat results across sites and operators against reliability and affordability thresholds set beforehand. This would define which patients and settings the service can safely support.

uncertain: The necessary follow-up length and acceptable differences from existing treatment remain to be defined.
Cost boundaries and thresholds for reliability and affordability remain to be agreed before evaluation.
It remains unclear how performance and costs would change across patient needs and local service conditions.

page.title: Portable dialysis below US$5 per day
page.definition: A transportable system would remove waste and excess fluid through an external blood filter (hemodialysis) or the abdominal lining (peritoneal dialysis). It would meet the Affordable Dialysis Prize targets: manufacture below US$1,000 at scale, treatment below US$5/day, solar operation and water from any source, with the safety and effectiveness of existing dialysis.

goal.need: A 2015 systematic review estimated that at least 2.284 million people might have died prematurely in 2010 because kidney replacement was inaccessible. Its conservative model placed the untreated population at 1.907 million in Asia and 432,000 in Africa. The authors identified lower-cost treatment and prevention as responses to this access gap.

figures.caption: Worldwide provision and estimated need for kidney replacement in 2010
figures.note: Kidney replacement includes dialysis and transplantation. These estimates describe 2010.

completion.title: A portable dialysis system meets the Affordable Dialysis Prize's cost, power, water and clinical targets.
completion.criterion: A functioning portable dialysis system meets the published prize targets together: manufacturing cost below US$1,000 at scale; treatment running cost below US$5/day; operation on solar power using any water source; and safety and effectiveness equal to existing dialysis systems. Portability follows KHI terminology: transportability that permits treatment beyond the home and clinic.
completion.set_by: International Society of Nephrology, Asian Pacific Society of Nephrology and The George Institute for Global Health, Affordable Dialysis Prize established in 2015; objectives restated by ISN in 2018. Portability terminology: Kidney Health Initiative.
completion.threshold_quote: It needed to cost less than US$1000 to build at scale and provide treatment for less than $5 a day
completion.basis: The prize couples numerical cost targets and specified power and water capabilities with the safety and effectiveness of existing dialysis. Its award announced on March 10, 2016 selected a design while prototype work was still underway. The design award therefore does not establish that a functioning clinical system meets the targets.

milestones.title: A dialysis prototype passes functional and safety testing for its intended operating environment.
milestones.criterion: The prototype performs as designed in functional testing, and its hazard analysis, electrical-safety and electromagnetic-compatibility testing support the intended environment of use. Hemodialysis precedent: SC+ passed bench validation supporting its 2024 home-use submission. Peritoneal-dialysis precedent: Liberty PDx's 2014 submission documents design verification, electrical safety, biocompatibility and usability testing.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Hemodialysis Delivery Systems guidance, section VIII; this recommendation was written for hemodialysis. The Liberty PDx clearance documents the corresponding performance-testing stage for peritoneal dialysis.
milestones.threshold_quote: functional testing that demonstrates that the device performs as designed and expected;

milestones.title: A dialysis system delivers treatment in people with initial safety and device function assessed.
milestones.criterion: A human feasibility study demonstrates dialysis delivery and assesses initial safety and device function. Hemodialysis: Gura's 2016 study enrolled 7 people; 5 completed 24 hours; technical faults stopped the study. Neokidney's 2024 abstract reports 3 people completing 2-hour treatments without adverse events. Through August 31, 2026, RENEW-HD included 29 people and 474 assisted in-center sessions without serious adverse device effects. Both Neokidney reports are conference abstracts, not peer-reviewed full papers. Peritoneal dialysis: AWAK's 2022 paper reports 15 people receiving up to 9 treatments over 72 hours, no serious adverse events and abdominal pain/discomfort in 60%.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 2013 guidance on early feasibility medical-device studies; this development stage applies across device types.
milestones.threshold_quote: Early feasibility studies allow for early clinical evaluation of devices to provide proof of principle and initial clinical safety data.

milestones.title: Patients or care partners deliver prescribed dialysis at home in a clinical investigation.
milestones.criterion: After training, patients or care partners deliver prescribed dialysis at home; comparison with in-clinic treatment evaluates adverse events, delivered dose and scheduled-treatment reliability. Hemodialysis: HOME RUN evaluated 32 participants; weekly standardized Kt/V, a dimensionless urea-removal dose, exceeded 2.1 in both settings. Peritoneal dialysis: EM-POC's 2025 paper reports 3 users filling 60 bags at home; 2 bags had detectable endotoxin. The fluid was not used for dialysis, so this result does not establish home treatment.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Nocturnal Home Hemodialysis IDE guidance, section 5. The published clinical-use criterion was written for nocturnal hemodialysis; it supplies no peritoneal-dialysis success margin.
milestones.threshold_quote: the subject’s or care partner’s ability, after appropriate training, to conduct the prescribed treatments in a nocturnal home hemodialysis setting.

milestones.title: A dialysis system receives FDA clearance with home treatment included in its indications.
milestones.criterion: FDA issues a marketing-clearance letter whose indications explicitly include home treatment, following substantial-equivalence review. Hemodialysis: SC+ received home-use clearance on November 1, 2024, for trained patients with trained care partners. Peritoneal dialysis: Liberty PDx received clearance including home use on July 30, 2014. These decisions establish the home-use authorization stage for those systems.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 510(k) substantial-equivalence process and the home-use indications enclosed with individual clearance decisions.
milestones.threshold_quote: This order "clears" the device for commercial distribution

not_found: No published demonstration was located that combines the prize's cost limits, solar operation, source-water capability and comparative clinical performance in one functioning system.
The prize documents located do not define clinical comparison margins, follow-up duration, complete treatment-cost boundaries or inflation adjustments.
No externally set population-coverage threshold for worldwide delivery was located in the prize, KidneyX or KHI materials.
A published peritoneal-dialysis counterpart to FDA's nocturnal-hemodialysis clinical-use criterion was not located.
The AWAK publisher page supplied the abstract but restricted access to the full article.
